div.div:
- `df.groupby('key')` returns `DataFrameGroupBy`.
- `df.groupby('key')['col-name']` returns `SeriesGroupBy`
- GroupBy object Does NO actual computation until aggregation is applied
- It supports iteration. Use as last option. `for key_name, group_df in df.groupby('key'):`
- Dispatch methods: any method not explicitly implemented by the GroupBy object will be passed through and called on each individual group (df or series objects). E.g. `df.groupby(key)[col-name].describe()`

- Think of pivot table as a multidimensional version of GroupBy aggregation
- Both are same:
`titanic.groupby(["sex", "class"])["survived"].aggregate("mean").unstack()`
`titanic.pivot_table("survived", index="sex", columns="class")`

div.div:
1. one-to-one: key column do not contain duplicate entries. Very similar to column concatenation.
2. many-to-one: one of the two key columns contains duplicate entries. Resulting DataFrame will preserve those duplicate entries as appropriate.
3. many-to-many: Both key columns contains duplicate entries. Similar to DB CROSS JOIN.

div.div:
- In pandas, a time series is a sequence of data points in chronological order, where the index of the DataFrame or Series is a time-aware index, typically a DatetimeIndex
- It is build on Python native `datetime` package & Numpy's `numpy.datetime64` & `numpy.timedelta64`
- Fundamental data structures for working with time series data: timestamp (represents a specific point in time), period (represents a fixed interval of time) & time-delta (represents a length of time). (SEE TABLE under ## Pandas Time Series)

- Shifting: It is the process of moving data backward or forward in time
- Rolling/Windowing: Creates a moving or "rolling" window of a specified size and then performs a calculation on the data within that window

div.div:
- `eval()` & `query()` allow you to directly access C-speed operations without costly allocation of intermediate arrays
- They rely on `Numexpr` package
- These functions are faster and uses much less memory
- `mask = (x > 0.5) & (y < 0.5)` is roughly equivalent to 3 intermediate steps `tmp1 = (x > 0.5); tmp2 = (y < 0.5); mask = tmp1 & tmp2`

div.div:
- `query()` is used for filtering operation
- comes in 1 flavour: `df.query()`
- `df.query` is needed since `pd.eval('df[(df.A < 0.5) & (df.B < 0.5)]')` can't be expressed using the `DataFrame.eval()`
- Similar to eval(), local variable can be used inside query() by preceding variable name with '@'
